claims.text: The initial alloy is as-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr.
As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room and elevated temperatures.
The proposed intervention is to reduce the Hf atomic ratio by nearly 50% while preserving the relative proportions of Mo, Ta, Ti, and Zr.
Reducing the Hf fraction will lower the density of HfMoTaTiZr.
The reduced-Hf alloy will preserve strength at room temperature and near 1000 °C.
Removing some Hf decreases the alloy's average atomic mass.
Reducing Hf will not adversely alter the single-phase BCC structure.
The remaining refractory elements will maintain grain size and phase stability after Hf reduction.
Hf is a high-density constituent of the alloy.
Reducing the amount of high-density Hf lowers alloy mass per unit volume.
Prior evidence indicates that decreasing Hf content can increase alloy strength.
Preserving the ratios of Mo, Ta, Ti, and Zr will leave high-temperature stability and strength largely unaffected.
The modified alloy will have comparable yield and ultimate strength at room temperature.
The modified alloy will have comparable yield and ultimate strength at approximately 1000 °C.
Hf reduction may slightly improve strength or cause no significant strength loss because of microstructural stability.
A representative room-temperature strength baseline is approximately 970 MPa.
The intervention remains effective from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C provided that the alloy remains single-phase BCC and grain coarsening is controlled.
Laser melting deposition can refine grains and address microstructural coarsening in a reduced-Hf/reduced-Ta refractory alloy.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and experimental design say that the concentrations of Mo, Ta, Ti, and Zr remain unchanged, whereas the intervention says only their relative proportions remain constant. In an atomic-percent composition, reducing Hf necessarily increases the normalized atomic percentages of the other elements, so their absolute concentrations cannot all remain unchanged.
